1.c4 e5.name: English Opening: King's English Variation
1.c4 e5.background: Also called the Reversed Sicilian, because it is a Sicilian Defence with the colours reversed; Kasparov and Keene's Batsford Chess Openings (1982) calls it the King's English. In Modern Chess Openings (14th edition, 1999), Bruce Leverett wrote that it is natural to treat the English as a Sicilian reversed, but that the results are often surprising.
1.c4 e5.strategy: Occupies the centre at once and controls d4 and f4, so White cannot easily play d4. White has the extra tempo and a grip on d5, where a knight backed by the c4-pawn is strong, while Black has the firm centre pawn.

1.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and controls d5 and e4 without committing a pawn, so Black can wait and choose a set-up once White shows his plan. White keeps the choice too: a quiet flank game, or a broad pawn centre at once, which Black must then challenge.

1.c4 c5.strategy: Contests d4 just as White's pawn contests d5, so the structure stays balanced and White's extra tempo is the main asset. Either side can strike with the d-pawn at the right moment, and that break shapes the game: it opens the centre, while without it the play is slow manoeuvring.

1.c4 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with pawn support, so that cxd5 can be met by ...exd5 with a firm centre, and keeps the development of Black's pieces flexible. The bishop on c8 stays shut in for a while, the usual price of this solid set-up, and White has many ways to change the character of the game, so Black must choose the move order with care.

1.c4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a solid pawn chain while keeping the c8-bishop free to develop before ...e6. The price is that the queen's knight loses c6 and often develops to d7, so Black's play is solid rather than active, and White decides how sharp the game becomes.

1.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 on the long diagonal and postpones every central decision. Black can still strike later in the centre or keep the fianchetto set-up. White may build a big centre at once, so Black must be ready to attack it.

1.c4 Nc6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Lithuanian Variation
1.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and prepares ...e5. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so Black cannot build with it, and 2.d4 e5 3.d5 gains space with tempo. Sound, but it offers nothing the main replies do not.

1.c4 f5.name: English Opening: Anglo-Dutch Defence
1.c4 f5.strategy: Controls e4 and aims for a Dutch-style set-up. Black gets sharp play and kingside attacking chances, but weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and the e6 square. White can fight for e4 with a bishop on g2.

1.c4 d5.name: English Opening: Anglo-Scandinavian Defence
1.c4 d5.background: Thought of as inferior to the Scandinavian Defence because White exchanges its c-pawn for Black's centre pawn. It is seldom played, though it may transpose into the Queen's Gambit or the Réti Opening.
1.c4 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once, but after 2.cxd5 White has traded a flank pawn for Black's centre pawn. Recapturing costs time: 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 drives the queen away, and after 2...Nf6 the knight that retakes on d5 can be chased by Nc3 and e4.

1.c4 b6.name: English Defence
1.c4 b6.background: Also reached by 1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6. The Leicester player P. N. Wallis investigated it in the late 1940s and early 1950s, and the English grandmasters Tony Miles and Jonathan Speelman have used it successfully.
1.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, fighting for e4 along the long diagonal instead of occupying the centre. White may build a broad pawn centre, which Black then tries to undermine with pawn breaks and piece pressure. Double-edged: if the undermining fails, White's space tells.

1.c4 d6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 and frees the c8-bishop, but blocks the f8-bishop and takes less space than ...e5 at once, so White can claim the centre at once. Sound but modest.

1.c4 g5.name: English Opening: Myers Defence
1.c4 g5.background: Named after Hugh Myers, who advocated it in print and in actual play. It is intended as an improved Grob's Attack, and John L. Watson considers it playable in his 1981 Batsford book on the English Opening.
1.c4 g5.strategy: Gains kingside space and prepares ...Bg7, aiming at d4 and b2 along the long diagonal. The pawn is loose: after 2.d4 the bishop on c1 attacks it, so Black must cover it or offer it as a gambit. The move weakens the dark squares around Black's king but is not refuted by force.

1.c4 b5.name: English Opening: Jaenisch Gambit
1.c4 b5.background: Named after Carl Jaenisch; also known as the Halibut Gambit. It can give Black good practical chances but is considered unsound at professional level.
1.c4 b5.strategy: Gives up the b-pawn for open lines: after 2.cxb5 a6 Black hopes for play on the a- and b-files. White does not need to take on a6: 3.e4 builds a centre and keeps the extra pawn, so the compensation falls short.

1.c4 Na6.strategy: A rim knight that claims no central square. White builds the centre at once, and Black must spend further tempi re-routing the knight, typically via c7.

1.c4 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 from a rim square, but 2.d4 already threatens Bxh6, after which ...gxh6 wrecks the kingside pawns. The knight costs time and the centre is left to White.

1.c4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 but does nothing for the centre or for development. White simply takes space or develops while Black has made a slow queenside move.

1.c4 a5.strategy: Stops b4 but is a slow flank move that permanently weakens b5 and does nothing for the centre. White simply occupies the centre.

1.c4 f6.strategy: Takes e5 and g5 but blocks the knight's best square on f6 and weakens the e8-h5 diagonal in front of the king. It develops nothing, and White takes the centre at once.

1.c4 h6.strategy: A waiting move that only takes g5 from White's bishop. It develops nothing and loses a tempo, and White keeps every central option.

1.c4 h5.strategy: Gains space on the kingside but weakens g5 and g6 and does nothing for the centre or development. White takes the centre at once.

1.c4.name: English Opening
1.c4.background: Named after Howard Staunton, the English player regarded as the unofficial world champion of his time, who played it in his 1843 match against Saint-Amant and at London 1851, the first international tournament. It caught on only in the 20th century; Botvinnik, Karpov, Kasparov and Carlsen have all used it in world championship matches.

1.c4 d5 2.cxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn that challenges c4: White trades a flank pawn for Black's central one. Black must either spend time winning the pawn back or pay for development with it, and that is why White keeps a small edge.

1.c4 d5 2.d4.strategy: Switches to a classical pawn centre: c4 hits d5 while d4 claims the centre, so White fights for it with two pawns instead of one. Black may take on c4 or hold d5, and the game turns into a well-trodden queen's-pawn structure, level but healthy.

1.c4 d5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops first and leaves the tension on c4 to Black: the knight covers d4 and e5, and if Black takes on c4 White can regain the pawn with a lead in development. Quiet, flexible positions follow, in which White has no early edge but no weaknesses either.

1.c4 d5 2.cxd5 Qxd5.strategy: Wins the pawn back at once and keeps the structure healthy. The price is an early queen outing: White gains a tempo by developing with an attack on it, and keeps a small lead in development.

1.c4 d5 2.cxd5 Nf6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Scandinavian Defence, Schulz Gambit
1.c4 d5 2.cxd5 Nf6.strategy: Attacks the pawn on d5 with a developing move, so Black gets the pawn back or gets quick development for it. White can ignore the attack or defend the pawn, and any edge White keeps is slight.

1.c4 d5 2.cxd5 e6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Scandinavian Defence, Löhn Gambit
1.c4 d5 2.cxd5 e6.strategy: A gambit: Black leaves the d5 pawn and opens the diagonal for the c8 bishop, hoping for quick development. If White takes on e6, Black recaptures but is still a pawn down, and the activity gained does not obviously pay for it.

1.c4 d5 2.cxd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops with an attack on the queen, so Black must lose another tempo. White leaves the opening with a lead in development and a small edge that Black has to neutralise.

1.c4 d5 2.cxd5 Qxd5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and blocks the queen's diagonal to g2, keeping c3 free for the other knight. It does not hit the queen, so Black keeps a free move: sound, but less ambitious than the immediate attack.

1.c4 d5 2.cxd5 Qxd5 3.e3.strategy: Opens the king's bishop and supports a later d4, a quiet developing move. It does not hit the queen, so the early pressure on it is given up and Black can bring pieces out around it.

1.c4 d5 2.cxd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qa5.name: English Opening: Anglo-Scandinavian Defence, Malvinas Variation
1.c4 d5 2.cxd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qa5.strategy: Steps aside to a square where the queen eyes the c3-knight and the a2-pawn, and pins the knight once White's d-pawn moves. The queen is safe, but 4.d4 builds a strong centre and the queen has little to do on a5, so White leads in development and space.

1.c4 d5 2.cxd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qd8.strategy: Returns the queen home, so Black has spent two moves on it while White develops with a lead. Nothing is weakened, but it is passive: White can build a broad pawn centre at leisure.

1.c4 d5 2.cxd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qd6.strategy: Keeps the queen in the centre and loses the least time. Nb5 hits it and eyes c7, but the queen steps aside with c7 still guarded, so White gains little. Black accepts a small lead in development for White in return for a sound structure with no weaknesses.

1.c4 e5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight toward d5 and e4, so that knight and c-pawn together control d5. White keeps the centre under pressure from the flank and can still choose between a slow, closed set-up and a more active one. The cost is commitment: ...Bb4 threatens to take the knight and double White's c-pawns.

1.c4 e5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2, which bears on d5 and b7 along the long diagonal, and leaves both knights uncommitted. Holding back Nc3 gives an early ...Bb4 no knight to hit, so White can choose the knights' squares later according to Black's set-up. The price is that d5 is less well covered, so ...d5 is easier for Black.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Nimzowitsch Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks e5 at once, so Black must defend the pawn or advance it. Advancing it with ...e4 kicks the knight away but leaves the pawn as a target, a sort of Alekhine's Defence with the colours reversed. White gets quick, natural development and keeps many set-ups available, while the e5-pawn ties Black to a decision.

1.c4 e5 2.a3.strategy: Prevents ...Bb4 and prepares b4 to gain queenside space, but develops nothing and adds nothing to the fight for the centre. Black can develop at leisure, so the move is sound but slow.

1.c4 e5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2 to pressure e5 along the long diagonal and keeps the choice of the other set-up moves open. Black holds e5 easily and develops, so the bishop gains little at first. Sound, but slower than the main moves.

1.c4 e5 2.d3.strategy: Supports a later e4 and opens the c1-bishop for a quiet set-up. It neither develops a piece nor adds pressure on d5, so Black develops freely and prepares ...d5. Sound, but passive.

1.c4 e5 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and prepares d4 to challenge e5. It does nothing against ...d5, which Black can prepare comfortably. Sound, but modest.

1.c4 e5 2.d4.strategy: Strikes at e5 at once and opens the centre. After 2...exd4 White has to recapture with the queen, which can be chased, or first play Nf3 and take back later, and Black develops freely. White's opening edge is gone, though the game stays balanced.

1.c4 e5 2.e4.strategy: Sets up the c4 and e4 pawn pair, which clamps d5. The cost is d4, which no white pawn can cover any more, and Black aims pieces at it while ...Nf6 hits e4. Sound, but it offers White no more than the main moves.

1.c4 e5 2.Qc2.strategy: Brings the queen out before the minor pieces to cover c4 and eye e4. After ...Nc6 the knight can jump to d4 or b4 and hit the queen with tempo, while White's development lags.

1.c4 e5 2.a4.strategy: Covers b5 but develops nothing and gives up b4 for good: with the a-pawn on a4 and the c-pawn on c4, no white pawn can ever cover the square. Black can put a bishop or a knight there and develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.f3.strategy: Takes f3 from the g1-knight and opens the e1–h4 diagonal, so ...Qh4+ forces g3. It covers e4 but develops nothing, and Black develops and takes the centre at leisure.

1.c4 e5 2.h3.strategy: A waiting move that loses a tempo: it prevents ...Bg4 but neither develops a piece nor contests the centre, so Black has a free hand.

1.c4 e5 2.h4.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rim and weakens g4 without helping the centre or development, so Black develops and takes space with ...d5.

1.c4 e5 2.Na3.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, heading for c2 or b5, and allows 2...Bxa3 3.bxa3, which leaves White with doubled, isolated a-pawns in return for the bishop pair. Otherwise the knight stands far from d5 and e4, and Black develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.Nh3.strategy: Heads for f4 or g5, but for now the e5-pawn covers f4 and the d8-queen covers g5, so the knight has no way forward from the rim. Black develops freely.

1.c4 e5 2.Qb3.strategy: Hits b7, which the c8-bishop guards, and brings the queen out early. 2...Nc6 followed by ...Nd4 chases it away with tempo, and White has lost time.

1.c4 e5 2.Qa4.strategy: Pins the d7-pawn against the king for a moment, but Black simply blocks the diagonal and takes the centre. The queen achieves nothing else on a4 and has spent a tempo that White's undeveloped pieces need.

1.c4 e5 2.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn: after 2...Bxb4 3.Bb2 the bishop hits e5, but Black holds the pawn without trouble. With the c-pawn already on c4, c3 is not available to chase the bishop, and Black stays a clean pawn up.

1.c4 e5 2.f4.strategy: Unlike the King's Gambit, it has no pawn on e4 to take over the centre: 2...exf4 simply wins a pawn and opens the e1–h4 diagonal against White's king. White must spend a tempo on Nf3 to stop ...Qh4+ before trying to win the pawn back.

1.c4 e5 2.g4.strategy: Leaves the g4-pawn without a defender and weakens f3 and h3. After 2...d5 the c8-bishop attacks g4, and 3.cxd5 Qxd5 also hits the h1-rook along the opened long diagonal.

1.c4 e5 2.c5.strategy: Pushes the c-pawn to a square where nothing defends it, and 2...Bxc5 wins it while developing the bishop toward f2. White has nothing to show for the pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nf6.strategy: The natural reply: Black develops with control of e4 and d5 and meets White's quiet second move without difficulty. The pawn on e5 holds the centre, and White has not claimed any space yet.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and opens the c8 bishop. Solid, but it fixes the pawn structure early and develops no piece, so Black is less flexible than after a developing move.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and defends e5 in one move, leaving the d-pawn free to choose later between a modest and an ambitious set-up. White's quiet second move has claimed no space, so Black can develop without worry.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to the centre, where with the c-pawn it controls d5 and e4. White's quiet set-up stays flexible: the next moves decide between a slow fianchetto and an active plan in the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight towards the centre and attacks e5, which the d6 pawn must keep defending. A natural developing move that commits White to nothing in the centre yet.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.d4.strategy: Strikes at e5 and opens the centre. If Black takes, the position becomes open and level, with White's quiet start having bought nothing special; if Black advances instead, the centre closes and Black gains space. A fair option, but it hands the choice to Black.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and adds protection to e5 while keeping the centre intact. The knight also watches d4 and b4, discouraging an early central break by White.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight, which controls e4 and d5 and so checks White's central expansion. A solid, flexible set-up in which Black builds up behind the e5 and d6 pawns and waits for White to show a plan.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares a bishop on g7 that supports the e5 pawn from behind. Sound but slow: it develops nothing yet, and the bishop is hemmed in by Black's own e5 pawn until that pawn moves or is exchanged.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.b3.strategy: Prepares the queen's bishop on the long diagonal. For now the knight on c3 stands in front of it, so the bishop only pressures e5 once that knight moves. A modest, flexible plan: White develops safely without challenging Black's centre.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight eyes e5, keeping Black's pieces tied to its defence, and the king's bishop is already free to develop. White keeps a flexible, harmonious set-up with a central pawn break in reserve.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.g3.strategy: Prepares the king's bishop on the long diagonal, where it works with the c4 pawn and the c3 knight against d5. A sound, unhurried set-up, but a slow one: it leaves Black time to organise the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.b3 Nf6.name: Amsterdam Attack
1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.b3 Nf6.strategy: Completes the development of both knights and takes control of e4 and d5, so White's e-pawn cannot advance for free. Black has a solid, flexible set-up with the centre held and no weaknesses.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.b3 Be7.strategy: Prepares to castle in the most economical way and keeps the d6 and e5 pawn chain compact. A solid waiting move: Black develops without weakening anything and lets White show its plans.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.b3 g6.strategy: Prepares a bishop on g7 behind the e5 pawn, which supports the centre but is hemmed in by its own pawn. Sound but passive: Black spends time on a bishop that has no target until the centre opens.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nf6 3.f4.strategy: Challenges e5 at once and aims at the f-file, but loosens White's pawns and opens the diagonal to the king. After ...exf4 exf4 Black develops with tempo and can strike in the centre, so White has the harder game for no reason.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight watches d5 and e4, so Black cannot grab space in the centre for free. White keeps a flexible, solid set-up and decides later how to challenge the centre. The game stays quiet and strategic rather than sharp.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nf6 3.d4.strategy: Strikes at e5 at once and claims the centre with a pawn pair. If Black takes and White retakes, White has two central pawns against one and presses on d5; if Black pushes the pawn to e4 instead, Black gains space and White has to undermine the advanced pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks e5, but Black answers by pushing the pawn to e4, which attacks the knight and gains space. The knight has to retreat or go to d4, where it is centralised but can be driven off again, so Black gets comfortable development against a slightly passive White set-up.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nf6 3.f4 exf4.strategy: Takes the pawn. If White retakes with the e-pawn, the position opens without harm to Black; if White offers the pawn as a gambit instead, Black has to answer quick development with care.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nf6 3.f4 d5.strategy: Hits the centre but leaves e5 en prise: 4.fxe5 wins the pawn and attacks the knight on f6 at the same time. The strike comes a move too late; Black should take on f4 first.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nf6 3.f4 e4.strategy: Gains space and takes d3 and f3 from White's pieces, but settles for a level game when the natural ...exf4 gives Black the better one. The advanced pawn is also a target White can undermine, so Black has to defend it with care.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nf6 3.f4 exf4 4.Nf3.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Kahiko-Hula Gambit
1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nf6 3.f4 exf4 4.Nf3.strategy: A gambit: White refuses to retake and develops, hoping open lines and a lead in development repay the pawn. Black can keep the pawn, and White's compensation does not obviously justify the sacrifice.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nf6 3.f4 exf4 4.exf4.strategy: The simple recapture: material is level and the f4 pawn controls e5 and g5. But the open e-file favours Black's quicker development and White's kingside is loose, so White has the harder game; no other move does better.

1.c4 e5 2.e3 Nf6 3.f4 exf4 4.d4.strategy: A second pawn offer: White ignores the f4 pawn and builds a broad centre. After ...fxe3 Bxe3 White is a pawn down but has the centre and open lines for the bishops; Black can develop with tempo, though simply recapturing on f4 is hardly better for White.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: The most natural reply: Black defends the pawn and develops a piece in one move, and the knight joins the fight for the centre. Black commits to nothing yet, so the set-up stays flexible. The price is that White keeps the initiative of the extra move and decides whether the game stays quiet or opens up.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 e4.name: English Opening: King's English Variation, Nimzowitsch-Flohr Variation
1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 e4.background: Wikibooks' opening theory notes that 2.Nf3 can lead to a reversed Alekhine's Defence of sorts if Black replies ...e4. In his 2024 Modern Chess course on 1.c4 e5, Grandmaster Boris Avrukh describes the position after 3.Nd4 Nc6 as a reversed Alapin in which Black has not played ...c6, and calls 4.e3 White's main move and the speciality of Alexander Rakhmanov.
1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 e4.strategy: Gains space and drives the knight from f3 at once; 3.Ng5 fails to 3...Qxg5, so the knight usually goes to the centre. The advanced pawn cramps White but also becomes a target that White can attack, so Black must keep supporting it. The game turns on whether that pawn holds or falls.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: Guards e5 with a pawn and frees the c8-bishop, but the f8-bishop is hemmed in. The structure is solid and passive; White can strike in the centre at once or develop calmly.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7.strategy: Guards e5 but blocks the f8-bishop and puts the queen where 3.Nc3 and Nd5 hit it with gain of tempo. The pawn is not lost, but Black falls behind in development.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6.strategy: Guards e5 with the queen but takes f6 from the knight and invites 3.Nc3 followed by Nd5 with gain of tempo. An early queen sortie that costs time without a clear purpose.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Bd6.strategy: Guards e5 but blocks the d-pawn, so the c8-bishop stays shut in and ...d5 is hard to prepare. White develops freely and takes the centre while Black's pieces lack good squares; no material is lost.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5.strategy: Leaves e5 unprotected as a trap: after 3.Nxe5 Black sacrifices on f2 and the queen's checks win the knight back. But White keeps the bishop pair, and can also decline the trap and simply develop.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Strikes at c4 at once, but 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains a tempo on the queen and leaves White ahead in development, while 3.Nxe5 is also available.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 f6.strategy: Guards e5 with a pawn but takes f6 from the knight and weakens the e6-square and the e8-h5 diagonal. White gets an easy lead in development.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Develops to the rim and heads for c5 or c7, but never guards e5: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the knight on a6 stays offside.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Qg5.strategy: Eyes g2, but the queen steps onto a square the f3-knight covers: 3.Nxg5 wins it for nothing.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Qh4.strategy: Puts the queen en prise to the f3-knight: 3.Nxh4 simply wins it.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Ke7.strategy: Forfeits castling and blocks the queen and the f8-bishop while e5 still hangs: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, with Black's king stuck in the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Be7.strategy: Does not guard e5, which the f3-knight takes: 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and the bishop cannot win it back.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Bb4.strategy: Pins the d2-pawn to the king but leaves e5 hanging: 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and the pin does not win it back.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Ba3.strategy: Throws the bishop away: 3.Nxa3 or 3.bxa3 wins a piece for nothing, and e5 is still hanging.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Puts a knight on the rim where it does not help guard e5: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn and Black is left with a poorly placed piece.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops, but the knight does not guard e5 and there is no e4-pawn to win back: 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn, and Black has open lines but no real compensation.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 Ne7.strategy: Heads for g6 or c6 but does not guard e5: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the knight's journey does not win it back.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 but ignores the threat on e5: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the a-pawn move does nothing for development or the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space but leaves e5 en prise: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the rook-pawn move plays no part in the fight for the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 against the long diagonal but never defends e5: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the bishop on b7 meets only a solid g2-pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn on the flank while e5 also hangs: 3.cxb5 or 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn at once, and the b-pawn thrust has no follow-up in the centre.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 but leaves e5 undefended: 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and ...Qa5 only hits the knight, which retreats with the extra pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 c5.strategy: Mirrors White's pawn but forgets e5: 3.Nxe5 takes it, and ...Nc6 trades the knight off while White keeps the extra pawn.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: Aims at space on the kingside but forgets the e5-pawn: 3.Nxe5 takes it, and a queen sortie to win it back only loses time.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto but leaves e5 en prise: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and White can support the knight in the centre, so Black is simply a pawn down.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: A lunge that loosens the kingside for good and still leaves e5 hanging: 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and the advanced g-pawn becomes a target.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: A waiting move that guards g5 but ignores the threat on e5: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the tempo contributes nothing to development.

1.c4 e5 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Pushes the rook-pawn for no reason and leaves e5 en prise: 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and the h-pawn does nothing for the centre or development.

1.c4 f5 2.Nf3.strategy: The flexible developing move: it controls e5 and d4 and keeps open the choice between a central pawn push and a kingside fianchetto. White sees how Black sets up the f5 structure before committing, and Black must be ready for several kinds of game.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3.strategy: Challenges the square Black's f5 pawn controls, e4, with a developed knight, and prepares a central pawn break there. A natural, solid move; White still decides later between a fianchetto and a central set-up.

1.c4 f5 2.e4.name: English Opening: Anglo-Dutch Defence, Hickmann Gambit
1.c4 f5 2.e4.strategy: Offers a pawn at once to open the centre and gain time for development. After ...fxe4 White has easy development and play against the e4 pawn, but Black simply keeps the extra pawn if he plays accurately. An offbeat surprise rather than a sound line.

1.c4 f5 2.g4.name: English Opening: Wade Gambit
1.c4 f5 2.g4.strategy: A pawn thrown at the f5 pawn to wreck Black's kingside: ...fxg4 simply wins a pawn, and White's own kingside pawn cover has gone with it. The idea is a quick attack on the open lines, but a pawn down with a loosened kingside White has little to show.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight where it joins the f-pawn in holding e4 and prepares castling. That makes White's pawn strike on e4 a sacrifice rather than a real break, and Black develops without concessions.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Claims e5 and frees the c8 bishop while keeping a compact structure. The cost is that e4 is watched by the f-pawn alone for now, so White can strike there at once, and Black needs the knight out quickly.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Prepares a solid pawn centre and opens the f8 bishop, a flexible set-up that suits a slow game. The price is the c8 bishop, shut in behind the pawns until the b-pawn moves.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.e4.name: English Opening: Anglo-Dutch Variation, Ferenc Gambit
1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.e4.strategy: Strikes at once on the square both black pieces guard, offering a pawn for open lines and quick development. Black takes and the knight on f6 defends the pawn, so White needs more than fast development to justify the sacrifice. Offbeat and risky.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares the kingside fianchetto: the bishop on g2 will press on the e4 square that Black's f-pawn and knight are fighting for, and White castles quickly. A slow game of pressure rather than an early break, with the centre left open to be settled later.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and covers e5 and d4, keeping both a central break and a kingside fianchetto available. Flexible, since it commits to nothing: Black decides which structure the f-pawn will lead to.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once and turns the game into the usual fight against the f5 set-up, with White's knight already on c3. White gains space and control of e5; Black answers with a solid pawn chain and tries to stake a claim on e4.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.e4 fxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn, which the knight on f6 defends, and plays for the extra material. The price is that the f-pawn leaves and opens the diagonal to the king, so Black must develop and castle with care.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.e4 d6.strategy: Declines the pawn and keeps the structure compact, with the c8 bishop free to recapture on f5 if White takes there. Black forgoes the extra pawn for safety, and White keeps a pawn on e4 with more space.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.e4 e6.strategy: Declines the pawn, but after 4.exf5 exf5 the f5-pawn is short of defenders: the c8-bishop is shut in behind d7, so 5.Bd3 hits it at once and Black must spend time or lose it. That leaves Black passive and White with the easier game.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.e4 fxe4 4.g4.name: English Opening: Porcupine Variation
1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.e4 fxe4 4.g4.strategy: Threatens g5 to chase the knight and grabs kingside space, but it loosens White's kingside while a pawn down already. The second pawn is poisoned: ...Nxg4 loses a knight to Qxg4. A sharp gambit that is playable, though riskier than the quiet 4.d3.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.e4 fxe4 4.Qe2.strategy: Aims to regain the pawn at once, and does, but the queen blocks the king's bishop. After 4...Nc6 5.Nxe4 e5 Black builds a strong centre with tempo, so White pays more in development than the pawn is worth.

1.c4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.e4 fxe4 4.d3.strategy: Attacks the e4-pawn a second time and opens the c1-bishop's diagonal. Black can keep the extra pawn, but White's lead in development and the open lines make up for it, so the game stays level. The natural way to play for the pawn.

1.c4 g5 2.d4.strategy: Hits the unprotected g5 pawn at once: the c1 bishop now eyes it and nothing defends it. White also claims the centre with a pawn while Black's kingside is overextended, so this is the most testing reply.

1.c4 g5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks the g5 pawn at once. If Black pushes it, the knight lands on a fine central post on d4, and the advanced pawn becomes a target; if Black defends, White has developed for free.

1.c4 g5 2.Nc3.strategy: A calm developing move that does not hit g5, so Black has time to support the pawn and settle in. Sound, but it gives up the chance to punish the advanced pawn at once.

1.c4 g5 2.d4 Bg7.name: English Opening: Myers Gambit
1.c4 g5 2.d4 Bg7.strategy: Gives up the g-pawn for pressure on d4 and the long diagonal. After 3.Bxg5 c5 Black hits d4 at once, and the pawn buys real play, though White keeps the better game. A gambit that is playable but not the safest.

1.c4 g5 2.d4 e5.name: English Opening: Zilbermints Gambit
1.c4 g5 2.d4 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn to open the queen's diagonal, so the queen now defends g5, and the f8 bishop's diagonal. White just takes the pawn and Black has too little for it, so the gambit is dubious.

1.c4 g5 2.d4 h6.strategy: Defends the pawn with a pawn, so Bxg5 now loses the bishop to hxg5. Black keeps the extra space on the kingside without material loss, but White still gets the stronger centre and a small, lasting edge.
